extracted.intended_audience: journalists, communication professionals, and the general public seeking appropriate and accurate language when writing or talking about people living with disabilities
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for journalists and communicators on appropriate terminology, phrasing, capitalization, and when to disclose disabilities in news and other reporting. Covers many specific disability-related terms with background, NCDJ recommendations, and AP style notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose / scope of the guide
rubrics_metrics.description: Intended for journalists, communication professionals and the general public seeking appropriate and accurate language when writing or talking about people living with disabilities. Entries include a definition, summary of how the term is used/viewed by disability groups, AP Style guidance when available, and an NCDJ recommendation aiming for accuracy and balance between clarity and sensitivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the guide's recommendations to choose neutral, precise, and respectful language; consult AP style notes where provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Able-bodied
rubrics_metrics.description: Background: term used to describe someone who does not identify as having a disability; some oppose it because it implies people with disabilities lack 'able bodies'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: Prefer 'non-disabled' or the phrase 'does not have a disability' as a more neutral choice. 'Able-bodied' is appropriate in some contexts (e.g., government reports on proportion of able-bodied members in the workforce). In some cases 'typical' can be used to describe a non-disabled condition. AP style: Not addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abnormal / abnormality
rubrics_metrics.description: Background: acceptable for scientific/medical phenomena; derogatory when used to describe a person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: Use 'abnormal'/'abnormality' for scientific phenomena (e.g., 'abnormal curvature of the spine'), but avoid using 'abnormal' to describe a person. Avoid calling someone a 'normal person' (use 'typical'). Be cautious with 'abnormal behavior'—explain meaning in context. AP style: Not addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Addict / addiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Background: addiction is a neurobiological disease; APA recommends avoiding label 'addict' and using people-first language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: Prefer 'someone with a drug addiction' or 'someone with an alcohol problem.' Use 'recovering' or 'in recovery from' when appropriate. Avoid 'clean'/'dirty' for drug test results; state 'tested positive for (drug)'. AP style: Not addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Afflicted with / stricken with / suffers from / victim of
rubrics_metrics.description: Background: these phrases assume suffering or reduced quality of life and may not apply to every person with a disability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: Use neutral language and simply state the facts (e.g., 'He has muscular dystrophy'). AP style: Conforms to AP guidance to avoid descriptions that connote pity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alcoholic / alcoholism
rubrics_metrics.description: Background: alcoholism is a disease; people-first language is recommended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: Refer to someone as 'someone with an alcohol problem' or 'someone with alcoholism.' Use 'recovering' for someone overcoming addiction. AP style: Conforms to AP.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alcoholics Anonymous (AA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Background: AA emphasizes anonymity; membership disclosure should be handled carefully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: Disclose membership only if essential; consider using first names for members unless context requires otherwise. Apply same consideration to other 12-step programs. AP style: 'AA' acceptable on second reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alzheimer's disease
rubrics_metrics.description: Background: progressive, fatal disease causing degeneration of nerve cells; most common form of dementia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: Use 'Alzheimer's disease' (never 'Alzheimer's'). Disclose an individual's diagnosis only if relevant and formally diagnosed; use 'someone who has Alzheimer's disease' rather than 'suffers from' or 'afflicted with.' Conforms to AP style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Background: federal civil rights legislation addressing discrimination on basis of disability in various areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: Use full name on first reference; 'ADA' acceptable on second. AP style: Not addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: American Sign Language (ASL) / signer / interpreter
rubrics_metrics.description: Background: ASL is a full language; 'signer' and 'interpreter' differ—interpreter has specialized training.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: Specify 'American Sign Language' on first reference (capitalize all three words); 'ASL' acceptable on second. Use 'interpreter' only for those with advanced training; Registry of Interpreters for the Deaf has a searchable database. AP style: Not addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amputation / amputee
rubrics_metrics.description: Background: amputation is removal of an extremity; 'amputee' is acceptable for someone who has undergone amputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: 'Someone with an amputation' or 'amputee' are both acceptable. AP style: Not addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Asperger's syndrome
rubrics_metrics.description: Background: autism spectrum disorder on the 'high functioning' end; named for Hans Asperger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: Refer to someone as having Asperger's syndrome only if relevant and formally diagnosed. If diagnosed, use 'a person diagnosed with Asperger's syndrome' or 'a person with Asperger's syndrome.' Otherwise follow autism/autism spectrum disorder guidelines. Note: 'syndrome' not capitalized. Conforms to AP.

rubrics_metrics.name: ADD / ADHD
rubrics_metrics.description: Background: attention-deficit disorders with common symptoms of restlessness and difficulty focusing; debate exists around diagnosis accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: Refer to someone as having ADD/ADHD only if relevant and formally diagnosed. Use full names on first reference and acronyms (ADD, ADHD) on second. AP style: Not addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Autism / autism spectrum disorder
rubrics_metrics.description: Background: group of complex disorders affecting brain development with variable symptoms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: Refer to someone as having autism spectrum disorder only if relevant and formally diagnosed. Ask individuals how they prefer to be described; if in doubt, use people-first language ('a person with autism spectrum disorder'). AP style: Autism acceptable as umbrella term; does not address 'autistic' as adjective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bipolar disorder
rubrics_metrics.description: Background: a mental illness characterized by intense mood episodes; formerly manic depression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: Refer to someone as having bipolar disorder only if central to the story and formally diagnosed; do not use 'bipolar' colloquially to mean rapidly changing. See also depression. AP style: Not addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blind / limited vision / low vision / partially sighted / visually impaired
rubrics_metrics.description: Background: 'legally blind' denotes 20/200 visual acuity; many with vision loss are not blind; preference varies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: Use 'blind' only for complete loss of sight and 'legally blind' for almost complete loss; otherwise ask the person which term they prefer. Common acceptable terms: limited vision, low vision, partially sighted (British usage), visually impaired. AP style: AP describes 'blind' as complete loss and suggests 'visually impaired' or 'person with low vision' for others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cerebral palsy
rubrics_metrics.description: Background: neurological disorders appearing in infancy/early childhood permanently affecting movement and coordination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: Use 'someone with cerebral palsy' followed by a short explanation of the condition; ask person what terms they prefer. 'Spastic' may be used medically (spastic cerebral palsy), but avoid using 'spastic' or 'spaz' as derogatory terms. AP style: Not addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cochlear implant
rubrics_metrics.description: Background: electronic device to help deaf/hard-of-hearing people understand speech; does not fully restore hearing and has cultural controversy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: Avoid describing it as 'corrective' or restoring a deaf person to mainstream society; define it as an electronic device that can assist in understanding speech. AP style: Not addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congenital disability
rubrics_metrics.description: Background: disability present since birth (e.g., Down syndrome).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: Prefer 'a person with a congenital disability', 'has had a disability since birth', or 'was born with a disability.' Name the specific disability only when pertinent; avoid 'defect'/'birth defect'/'defective'. AP style: Not addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crazy / loony / mad / psycho
rubrics_metrics.description: Background: derogatory when applied to people with mental illness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: Avoid these words in reporting on mental illness unless part of an essential quote. AP style: Conforms to AP guidance (implicit).

rubrics_metrics.name: Deaf
rubrics_metrics.description: Background: some with hearing loss affiliate with Deaf community and prefer 'deaf'; capitalization signals cultural identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: Use lowercase when referring to hearing-loss condition or to a person who prefers lowercase; capitalize 'Deaf' for those identifying with Deaf culture. Use 'deaf' as an adjective, not a noun; alternative phrasing: 'woman who is deaf' or 'boy who is hard of hearing.' AP style: AP uses 'deaf' for total hearing loss and 'partially deaf' or 'partial hearing' for others, calling for lowercase 'd' in all usages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deaf-blind
rubrics_metrics.description: Background: indicates some loss of both vision and hearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: Use the terms the person prefers. AP style: Not addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deaf and dumb / deaf-mute
rubrics_metrics.description: Background: historical terms implying inability to speak; inaccurate and offensive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: Avoid these terms as they are often inaccurate and offensive. Conforms to AP style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defect / birth defect
rubrics_metrics.description: Background: words imply imperfection and can be offensive when describing disabilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: Avoid using 'defect' or 'defective' when describing a disability; instead state the nature of the disability or injury. AP style: Not addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deformed / deformity
rubrics_metrics.description: Background: 'deformity' has negative connotations and many object to its use describing people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: Avoid using 'deformed' as an adjective to describe a person. 'Deformity' can be used in some contexts (e.g., a deformed limb) but preferable to describe the specific disability or cause. AP style: AP medical stories refer to 'deformity' or 'deformities' rather than calling an individual 'deformed.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Dementia / senility
rubrics_metrics.description: Background: dementia is a general term for decline in mental ability severe enough to interfere with daily life; Alzheimer’s disease is most common form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: Refer to someone as having dementia only if relevant and formally diagnosed; use people-first language ('a person with dementia'); avoid 'demented' or 'senile.' Reference specific disease when possible and do not shorten names like Huntington's or Parkinson's. AP style: Not addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depression
rubrics_metrics.description: Background: characterized by loss of interest, fatigue, concentration difficulties; proper name is major depressive disorder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: Refer to someone as having depression only if relevant and formally diagnosed; specify type if known. Terms like 'depressed' or 'depressive' acceptable in other contexts when diagnosis not claimed. AP style: Not addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Developmental disabilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Background: group of conditions arising due to impairments in physical, learning, language or behavior areas, usually manifesting before age 22.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: While acceptable to use the umbrella term, prefer naming the specific disability whenever possible. AP style: Not addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disabled / disability
rubrics_metrics.description: Background: describes functional limitations affecting major life activities; legal definitions vary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: Do not reference a person's disability unless clearly pertinent to the story. If pertinent, use people-first language (e.g., 'the writer, who has a disability'); refer to specific condition when possible; avoid lumping people as 'the disabled'—use 'the disability community' or 'the disability activist' instead. Conforms to AP style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dissociative identity disorder (DID) / multiple personality disorder
rubrics_metrics.description: Background: characterized by emergence of two or more distinct personality states (alters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: Refer to someone as having dissociative identity disorder only if relevant and formally diagnosed. Use 'dissociative identity disorder' (not 'multiple personality disorder'), avoid acronym 'DID', and use people-first language ('a person with dissociative identity disorder'). AP style: Not addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Down syndrome
rubrics_metrics.description: Background: congenital condition caused by extra full/partial copy of chromosome 21.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: (implied) Use appropriate, people-first phrasing and only name if pertinent; follow general guide conventions. AP style: (not shown in excerpt).

rubrics_metrics.name: Quadriplegia / people-first phrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: Background: (excerpt shows guidance near quadriplegia entry) people-first language preferred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: Use people-first language ('a person with quadriplegia') rather than adjectival form 'quadriplegic.' If individuals use reclaimed terms (e.g., 'quads'), use in quotes. AP style: Not addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retarded / mentally retarded (see related entries)
rubrics_metrics.description: Background: offensive term; see entries on mentally retarded, mentally disabled, intellectually disabled, developmentally disabled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: Avoid these terms; use respectful, modern terminology (see related entries).

rubrics_metrics.name: Schizophrenia / schizophrenic
rubrics_metrics.description: Background: severe chronic mental illness with distorted perceptions of reality; less than 1% prevalence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: Refer to someone as having schizophrenia only if relevant and formally diagnosed; use people-first language ('a person with schizophrenia' or 'a person diagnosed with schizophrenia') rather than 'a schizophrenic.' Do not use 'schizophrenic' colloquially. AP style: Classifies schizophrenia as a mental illness and cautions against using mental-health terms to describe non-health issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seizure (see epilepsy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Background: refer to epilepsy entry for seizures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: Follow epilepsy guidance (not included in excerpt).

rubrics_metrics.name: Service animal / assistance animal / guide dog / Seeing Eye dog
rubrics_metrics.description: Background: service animals are trained animals that perform tasks for people with disabilities; federal ADA definition covers trained animals regardless of licensing/certification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: 'Service animal', 'assistance animal' and 'guide dog' are acceptable; avoid 'Seeing Eye dog' because it's a registered trademark. Consider referring to the federal definition and be aware that licensure/certification is contentious in disability community. AP style: No entry; notes Seeing Eye dog trademark and suggests 'guide dog' instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short stature / dwarf / little person / midget
rubrics_metrics.description: Background: see related entry (short stature referenced to Dwarf/little person/midget).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: Use person-preferred terminology; avoid derogatory terms like 'midget.' (Specific guidance in dwarf/little person entry not in excerpt.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Spastic / spaz
rubrics_metrics.description: Background: linked to cerebral palsy; 'spastic' describes a type of cerebral palsy but is derogatory used as insult.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: Acceptable to refer to 'spastic cerebral palsy' medically; avoid calling someone 'spastic' or 'a spaz.' AP style: Not addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special / special needs / functional needs
rubrics_metrics.description: Background: 'special needs' historically used but now widely considered offensive/euphemistic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: Avoid 'special'/'special needs' when describing people or programs (except formal government names). Prefer to cite specific disability or use 'functional needs' if a term is required (e.g., 'addressing the functional needs of people with disabilities'). AP style: Not addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spina bifida
rubrics_metrics.description: Background: neural tube defect that can cause a range of complications from minor to severe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: Acceptable to describe 'someone with spina bifida' followed by a brief explanation of the condition. AP style: Not addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stuttering / stammering
rubrics_metrics.description: Background: stuttering is a speech disorder; DSM term 'childhood-onset fluency disorder' exists but not widely used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: Prefer 'stuttering' over 'stammering.' Do not label someone a 'stutterer'; use people-first language ('a person who stutters'). Refer to stuttering only if relevant to the story. AP style: Not addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tourette syndrome
rubrics_metrics.description: Background: neurological disorder with tics; terminology varies but many organizations use 'Tourette syndrome.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: Use 'Tourette syndrome' (no possessive or capitalization of 'syndrome'). Refer to someone as having it only if relevant and formally diagnosed; use people-first language; avoid acronym 'TS' as not widely known. AP style: Not addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment / treatment center / rehab center / detox center
rubrics_metrics.description: Background: 'treatment' defined as planned interventions (ASAM); treatment centers usually run by professionals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: 'Treatment' and 'treatment center' are acceptable; use 'treatment center' instead of 'rehab' or 'detox center.' A person enrolled should be called a 'patient.' AP style: Not addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vegetative state / comatose / non-responsive
rubrics_metrics.description: Background: vegetative state is absence of responsiveness; minimally conscious state indicates some awareness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: Prefer precise medical terminology; if not possible use 'comatose' or 'non-responsive.' If using 'vegetative state' use people-first language ('a person in a vegetative state') and avoid calling someone a 'vegetable' or 'veg.' AP style: Allows 'vegetative state' with a precise definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wheelchair / wheelchair-bound / confined to a wheelchair
rubrics_metrics.description: Background: mobility equipment is part of personal space; wheelchair users vary widely in abilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: Use 'someone who uses a wheelchair' and explain why equipment required; avoid 'confined to a wheelchair' or 'wheelchair-bound' as inaccurate and demeaning—wheelchairs empower mobility. Conforms to AP style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance: when to mention disability
rubrics_metrics.description: Background: 'relevant' means the disability should be mentioned only when it matters to the story; examples clarify borderline cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: Mention disability only if it affects the story's subject matter (e.g., blindness contributing to being stranded while hiking). In doubtful cases, ask the person involved. People complain when disability is mentioned when irrelevant. Use judgment: airplane noise story—do not mention wheelchair use; hiker stranded where blindness contributed—maybe mention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entry format requirement (definition/background/AP/NCDJ recommendation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each entry includes background, summary of community views, AP Style guidance when available, and the NCDJ recommendation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When consulting the guide, review all four components per entry (definition/background, community perspective, AP style note, NCDJ recommendation) to inform reporting choices.
